@RepEricBurlison Thank you for revealing the truth on ACA. The question below is critical to legislators who defend Obamacare.

So you don't know how insurance works.  

This framing is false, and it relies on cherry picked averages that deliberately ignore how the Affordable Care Act actually works.

First, the claim that enrollees paid 32 percent of premiums in 2014 versus 7 percent today is not a measure of fraud or illusion, it reflects policy choices Congress made to expand subsidies so coverage stayed affordable as premiums rose nationwide. Premium tax credits were modest in 2014 and were later expanded, first temporarily during the pandemic and then extended, precisely because unsubsidized premiums were pricing middle income families out of coverage. When subsidies increase, the enrollee share goes down by design. That is not a scam, it is the point of the law.

Second, taxpayers covering a large share of premiums is not new, unusual, or dishonest. Employer sponsored insurance is also heavily taxpayer subsidized through the tax exclusion for employer paid premiums, which costs the federal government well over $250 billion a year. Medicare is mostly taxpayer funded. Medicaid is overwhelmingly taxpayer funded. Calling subsidies a “scam” only when they help people who do not get insurance through an employer is ideological, not analytical.

Third, “millions aren’t even eligible” is misleading. Subsidies are income based, not universal, because the ACA was designed to target people who lack employer coverage and cannot afford full premiums. People above the income thresholds can still buy ACA plans, they just do so without subsidies, exactly like higher income workers do in employer plans through lost tax exclusions. That is not exclusion, it is means testing.

Fourth, this is health care coverage in every legally meaningful sense. ACA plans are required to cover essential health benefits, cap out of pocket costs, ban pre existing condition exclusions, and guarantee issue. Subsidies do not negate coverage any more than Medicare being publicly funded negates the fact that seniors receive health care.

What is really happening here is an argument against subsidized insurance, not a revelation of deception. If the standard is that coverage only “counts” when individuals pay the full sticker price, then Medicare, Medicaid, the VA, and employer sponsored insurance all fail that test. The ACA simply made the subsidy explicit instead of hiding it in the tax code.

If someone wants to argue that the United States should not subsidize health insurance at all, that is an honest debate. Pretending the ACA is uniquely fraudulent because it reduces what people pay out of pocket is not.
